issues.legal_issue: A purchaser does not breach a conditional undertaking to buy shares when the liquidators make an invalid tender that does not satisfy the agreed requirements.
material_facts: The undertaking required the liquidators to submit shares allotted to them with duly executed transfer forms and required contributories seeking payment to notify their intention and deliver their certificates and signed transfer forms.

The liquidators made a composite tender relying partly on letters of authority from contributories, but did not have the required authorities for all the shares and did not make clear that they were separately exercising their right to submit shares allotted to them.
The purchaser refused the tender and promptly explained that it was invalid.
issues.conclusion: The tender was invalid, and the purchaser did not breach the agreement by refusing it.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of the agreement must be applied as written. A party is not in breach for refusing a tender that does not satisfy the agreed requirements. The Court relied on its construction of the contractual clauses governing the tender; no earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this issue.

predicates.winding_up_share_sale_proceeding: The dispute concerns a sale or proposed sale of assets being dealt with in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.tender_requires_authority_and_transfer_d: The parties' agreement requires authority and specified transfer documents to accompany a tender of shares.
predicates.tender_lacks_required_authority: The tendering party does not have the required authority for some or all of the shares tendered.
predicates.tender_does_not_make_clear_which_contrac: The tendering party does not make clear the contractual basis on which it tenders some or all of the shares.

issues.definition: When a share tender in a winding-up sale lacks required authority or fails to identify the contractual right being exercised, refusal of that tender is not a contractual breach.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement requiring a purchaser to buy shares if they are offered does not itself give the purchaser a right to require that the shares be offered.
material_facts: The agreement required the purchaser to buy shares from contributories who chose to offer them within the specified period and to buy a specified number of shares from the liquidators if submitted.
The agreement did not require the contributories or liquidators to offer any shares to the purchaser.
The liquidators and contributories remained free to sell shares to others.
issues.conclusion: The agreement did not give the purchaser a right to acquire the shares from the contributories or liquidators.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the agreement as imposing an undertaking on the purchaser if the shares were offered, not an obligation on the contributories or liquidators to make an offer. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this issue.

predicates.winding_up_share_sale_proceeding: The dispute concerns a sale or proposed sale of assets being dealt with in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.purchaser_undertaking_is_conditional_on_: The purchaser promises to buy shares if they are offered or submitted under specified conditions.
predicates.no_contractual_duty_to_offer_shares: The agreement does not require the contributories or liquidators to offer shares to the purchaser.

issues.definition: A conditional promise to buy shares does not give the purchaser a right to compel an offer when the agreement imposes no duty to offer shares.

issues.legal_issue: A court supervising a winding-up sale may prefer an offer where the purchaser has acquired a preferential claim through the parties’ subsequent conduct and the competing offer is not better on the facts then before the court.
material_facts: After the dispute over the earlier tender, the purchaser waived his objections, offered to take all the shares for the agreed price, and delivered a cheque for the full amount.
A liquidator accepted the letters and cheque, cashed the cheque subject to approval by the other liquidator and the court, and gave the purchaser proxies for the shares.
The purchaser also undertook to pay the liquidators the declared dividend on the shares.
The competing offer was for the same price, and no higher offer was before the District Judge when he considered the offers.

The Supreme Court found that these events created an expectation amounting to an inchoate right, or at least a preferential claim, and that the District Judge had not exercised his discretion erroneously by accepting the purchaser’s offer.
issues.conclusion: The District Judge was justified in sanctioning the purchaser’s offer in preference to the competing offer.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the subsequent dealings as creating an inchoate right or preferential claim and held that the District Judge’s discretion was properly exercised on the facts before him. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this issue.

predicates.winding_up_share_sale_proceeding: The court is considering offers for property in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.purchaser_has_waived_objections_and_tend: The purchaser has withdrawn objections to the transaction and tendered the full purchase price.
predicates.liquidator_has_accepted_payment_subject_: A liquidator has accepted the purchaser’s documents or payment while making completion subject to the required approval.
predicates.competing_offer_is_not_better_on_record: On the evidence before the court at the time of decision, the competing offer is not shown to be more advantageous.

issues.definition: Where a purchaser waives objections and tenders full payment that a liquidator accepts subject to approval, the court may prefer that purchaser if the competing offer is not better on the record.

issues.legal_issue: As between a seller and purchaser of shares, a purchaser is entitled to dividends declared after the contract of sale unless the parties arrange otherwise, even if the seller remains the registered shareholder.
material_facts: The shares remained registered in the liquidators’ names when the purchaser agreed to give them the dividend declared at the company’s forthcoming annual meeting.
The offer was subject to court sanction, and the District Judge sanctioned the sale before the dividend was declared.
The purchaser’s undertaking to give the dividend to the liquidators meant that the liquidators would retain it, unlike under the competing offer.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s dividend undertaking made his offer more valuable to the liquidators and supported sanctioning it over the competing offer.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle stated in Palmer’s Company Law, 19th edition, page 205: as between buyer and seller, the buyer is entitled to dividends declared after the contract for sale unless otherwise arranged, although a transfer after declaration does not carry the dividend as against the company. The registered holder may therefore receive the dividend from the company but must account for it to the buyer; an agreement that the buyer will instead give it to the seller alters that position.

predicates.share_sale_contract_precedes_dividend_de: The contract for the sale of shares is made before the dividend is declared.
predicates.seller_remains_registered_holder: The seller remains the person recorded as the shareholder when the dividend is declared.
predicates.no_contrary_arrangement_exists: The buyer and seller have not agreed on a different allocation of the dividend.

issues.definition: When a share sale contract precedes declaration of a dividend, the buyer is entitled to that dividend as against the seller unless they have arranged otherwise.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of notice to contributories does not invalidate approval of a share sale when no higher price was reasonably apparent and their interests were represented by the information before the court.
material_facts: When the liquidators applied for approval, the market price was below the price offered by both prospective purchasers.
The liquidators and contributories were seeking to obtain the offered price, and the contributories had not indicated that a higher price could be obtained.
The later higher offers emerged only after the District Judge had made his decision.
issues.conclusion: There was no need in the circumstances to give the contributories notice of the application, and the District Judge could decide between the two offers before him.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that notice was not required in the circumstances because there was no apparent prospect of obtaining more than the offers before the District Judge and no material contention the contributories could have added to the information already presented. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this issue.

predicates.winding_up_share_sale_proceeding: The court is considering approval of a sale in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.contributories_not_notified: The contributories are not given notice of the application for approval.
predicates.no_higher_price_reasonably_apparent_at_h: At the time of the hearing, the available information gives no reasonable indication that a higher price can be obtained.
predicates.available_information_covers_contributor: The information before the court addresses the contributories’ relevant interests and the available offers.

issues.definition: If the contributories are not notified but no higher price is reasonably apparent and the available information covers their interests, the lack of notice does not invalidate approval.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not set aside a proper exercise of discretion in approving a winding-up sale on the basis of higher offers that arose after the decision under appeal.
material_facts: The District Judge approved one of two offers, neither of which exceeded the price then available in the market.
The contributories did not establish a prospect of a higher price until after the appeal had begun and the hearing had been adjourned.
Higher offers were then obtained from third parties, and the High Court ordered a public auction on that later evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the District Judge had not erred on the facts before him and that there was no prejudice to the contributories.
The High Court’s decision to order an auction was set aside.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the District Judge’s discretion or ordering a public auction on the basis of the later offers.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that an appeal may take account of later events only for moulding the relief to be granted, citing Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, 1940 FCR 84 at page 103 (AIR 1941 FC 5 at page 13). It held that later offers created after the decision did not justify overturning a proper exercise of discretion on the facts then before the District Judge.

rule.if: appeal_from_discretionary_sale_approval and original_decision_was_reasonable_on_record and no_prejudice_to_interested_contributors and higher_offers_arose_after_decision

predicates.appeal_from_discretionary_sale_approval: The proceeding is an appeal from a court’s discretionary approval of a sale in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.original_decision_was_reasonable_on_reco: The court making the original decision acted reasonably on the evidence and offers then before it.
predicates.no_prejudice_to_interested_contributors: The original decision did not prejudice the interests of the contributors to the company being wound up.
predicates.higher_offers_arose_after_decision: Higher offers became available only after the decision under appeal had been made.

issues.definition: On an appeal from discretionary sale approval, later offers do not justify overturning a reasonable original decision when interested contributors were not prejudiced.
